newsitem.title: CZECH REPUBLIC: TRADE MIN SAYS CZECHS WILL NOT ABANDON FREE MARKET.
newsitem.headline: TRADE MIN SAYS CZECHS WILL NOT ABANDON FREE MARKET.

text.p: The Czech Republic will not abandon its free market principles despite a burgeoning trade deficit and several other macro-economic problems, Industry and Trade Minister Vladimir Dlouhy said on Thursday.
Speaking at an economic forum attended by French President Jacques Chirac, Dlouhy said the transformation from a centrally-planned to free market economy had been successful.

Dlouhy rejected the view of many analysts that the economy was in trouble, given its record 1996 trade deficit of 160.3 billion crowns and recent data showing two consecutive months of contracting industrial sales and pressure on the state budget toward a deficit.
"The Czech economy is ready to face these pressures without abandoning its basic principles of liberal trade and pursuit of privatisation," he said.
"Some (analysts) say the economy is now in trouble, but 4.4 percent real GDP growth (in 1996) is not a sign of crisis. I reject all notions of a crisis in the Czech economy," he added.

Dlouhy admitted the trade deficit, which is projected to grow to some 215 billion crowns for 1997, was also a problem that needed to be addressed, but that a devaluation of the crown to spur exports was not an answer.
"I am sure that the solution of the massive (trade) deficit is not a devaluation which would only delay, and not solve the problem," he said.

After three years of a surplus, the budget dipped to a 1.56 billion crown shortfall in 1996. Parliament has passed a balanced budget for this year, though government officials say steps will need to be taken soon if the goal is to be achieved.
For the first two months of 1997, the budget was in deficit by some 8.5 billion crowns. The government has blamed a slowdown in the pace of economic growth and lower tax revenues for the deficit.
On Wednesday, Dlouhy said he did did not favour an import surcharge as a tool to fix the deficit.
He said would instead propose stricter adherence to existing import barriers, including enforcement of quality certification and other requirements.
